opening.headline: When the input is the same but the format is unstable and the facts are wrong, we will cover how to prescribe the cause by determining whether the cause is instructions, examples, or lack of evidence.
body: I summarized the same contract three times, once as a table, once as bullet points, and once as paragraphs. One of the responses contained termination conditions that were not in the contract. The problem of format being unstable and the problem of facts being incorrect may seem similar on the surface, but the causes are different and the solutions are different.

In this lesson, we first look at techniques for fixing output formats and structural methods to increase the consistency of repetitive tasks. Next, we cover the basic techniques for reducing false information, such as allowing 'if you don't know, you don't know', quoting the original text, and providing evidence, as well as advanced verification techniques that compare and doubt the results and how to deal with long output. At the end, error cases are classified by cause and questions regarding contract termination conditions are improved step by step.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain techniques to increase consistency and reduce hallucination
Can distinguish whether errors come from instructions, examples, or lack of evidence
The strength and scope of application of the means for fixing the format can be distinguished and explained.

screens.title: It's the same input, but the format is shaky and the facts are wrong.
screens.lead: This is a side-by-side scene showing the results of summarizing the same contract three times. Read below and think about what types of problems are in the mix.

visual.alt: A scene showing three summary results for the same contract entry side-by-side in different formats.

paragraphs: We gave a copy of the contract to an AI and had it summarize it three times with the same request. The first came back as a table, the second as a bulleted list, and the third as a paragraph. If it is the same request with the same input but the format is different each time, subsequent work to process the results becomes cumbersome.

There was also a bigger problem. The second response included termination terms that were not found anywhere in the contract. The reason why the format is unstable is because the shape was not told to the model, and the reason that non-existent conditions were included is because the model filled in plausible content without any basis.
Since these two have different causes, the treatments are also different. The question for this class is this. How do you tell whether an error comes from instructions, examples, or lack of evidence?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If I write longer instructions to fix the formatting problem, will the problem of non-existent termination conditions go away as well?

screens.outro: Now that we've distinguished between the two types of problems, let's think about an experience we've had.

screens.title: Recall the moment you experienced shaking
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had trouble post-processing the same request but with different result formats?
items.answer: This is especially inconvenient when transferring results to a table or transferring them to another tool. Format shakiness usually occurs when you don't give your model enough of what you want it to look like. In this lesson, we first look at how to precisely define the format and support it with examples.

items.prompt: Has the model ever added anything that wasn't in the document?
items.answer: This is a matter of fact, not form. This is a case where the model fills in plausible content even though there is no basis in the document. No matter how much we refine the formal instructions, this problem will not be solved, and the prescriptions will be directed towards requiring evidence.

items.prompt: Do you remember the model answering ‘I don’t know’?
items.answer: Such responses are rare. This is because the model usually moves in the direction you want to answer. Claude explains that simply providing permission to say you don't know can significantly reduce false information. We'll see how to do this in detail in the screen that follows.

screens.outro: First, let's look at the formal techniques.

screens.title: Fixed output format and example/prefill
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare how the response of the same input changes before and after formatting.

visual.alt: A comparison plot showing three different responses before formatting and three tables with the same columns after formatting.

states.label: Before formatting
states.body:
The request is one line: 'Summary this contract.' If you turn it three times with the same input, it will look like this.

- First: summary in paragraph form
- Second: bullet list
- Third: Table with different column names

If the shape of the summary is not given to the model, it picks the most likely shape each time. To a human, it's all a summary, but the subsequent work that carries over the results has to be retouched every time the shape changes.

states.label: After formatting
states.body:
Claude's article walks you through three basic means of increasing consistency:

**Define the format precisely.** You specify the output format you want with JSON, XML, or a custom template, and the model follows each format element.

**Limited to examples.** The document explains that giving examples of desired output is more effective than abstract instructions.

**Prefill the beginning of the response (prefill).** If you fill in the beginning of the assistant's turn (the model's turn to answer) in the format you want, the model will skip the friendly introduction and follow the structure you set.

```
| Articles | Key Takeaways | Confirmation required |
|------|---------------|-----------|
```

In models that support prefill, these headers can guide the start, but they do not guarantee output in the same rows. Although the three responses after designation have different contents, they have the same appearance, so post-processing only needs to be done once.

The means of fixing the form differ in their strength. The weakest is verbal instructions, followed by examples, and then pre-writing. The strongest one is Structured Output, which forces the structure of the output by passing the JSON schema to the API.

The OpenAI documentation explains that structured output is even guaranteed to follow the schema you provide, unlike JSON mode. However, the Gemini document advises you to verify the value in the app, as even if the output is grammatically correct JSON, it does not mean that the meaning of the value is correct.

Prefilling does not work for all models. Claude 4.6 and later models and Mythos Preview do not support prefilling the last assistant turn, and cannot be used with the structured JSON output feature. Therefore, first check whether it is supported in the documentation of the model you want to use.

screens.outro: Now that we have the format fixed, let's look at other ways to increase consistency across iterations.

ext.title: Anthropic Claude structured output document (compatible with prefill or not)
Anthropic Claude Prompt Best Practices (Prefill Support Scope)

screens.title: Search chaining, prompt chaining, and role retention
screens.lead: Select and expand each item to see how the technique works and when to use it. Expand all three items.

visual.alt: Illustration of the three technique cards of Search Linkage, Prompt Linkage, and Role Maintenance laid out horizontally.
labels: Based on a fixed set of information
Instead of writing long instructions, change the structure.

items.title: Linking searches: Basing them on a fixed set of information
items.body:
In tasks that require consistent context, such as chatbots or knowledge bases, responses are based on a fixed set of information rather than the model's memory. The Claude document explains this as a way to ensure context consistency through retrieval.

For example, if it is a chatbot that asks about company regulations, it finds the relevant regulation clause for each question, puts it in the prompt, and answers based on the contents. Then, the same basis is provided for the same question, so the answer does not waver. The key is not to rely on what the model appears to know.

items.title: Chaining Prompts: Breaking Complex Tasks into Subtasks
items.body:
Break complex tasks into smaller, coherent subtasks. Because each subtask receives the model's full attention, inconsistency errors that occur when iterating at scale are reduced.

For example, in contract review, instead of summarizing, determining risk, and suggesting modifications all at once, it is divided into 'step 1 clause extraction, step 2 risk classification, step 3 summary' and passes the output of the previous step as input to the next step. The format and standards for each step are clear, which reduces vacillation.

items.title: Maintaining a Role: Anchoring Your Personality with System Prompts
items.body:
Maintaining a consistent personality in role-based applications requires intentional prompting. First, defining the role and nature of the model with system prompts provides a solid foundation for consistent responses.

Second, prepare for possible scenarios. By providing prompts with a list of common situations and expected responses, you can train your dog to respond in a variety of situations without having to deviate from its role, the document explains.

The three techniques have something in common. These are all ways to change the structure, not to write longer instructions.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen consistency techniques, let's move on to techniques for reducing factual errors.

screens.title: Demand for evidence and ‘if you don’t know, you don’t know’
screens.lead: Select the arrows to move through each step to see the process of creating an answer tied to evidence.

visual.alt: An illustration in which quoted sentences are extracted from the original document and connected by lines to each claim in the answer.
labels: Do not use general knowledge outside of the document

steps.title: Step 1: Give permission not to know
steps.body: Claude's documentation tells you to give your model permission to say he doesn't know. It is said that this simple technique alone significantly reduces false information. For example, include one sentence: 'If it is not in the document, answer not in the document.' Without this permission, the model moves to fill in the blank.

steps.title: Step 2: Extract quotations from the original text.
steps.body: When dealing with long documents, approximately more than 20,000 tokens, I first extract verbatim quotes from the original text before starting the work. This ties the model's answers tightly to the actual text, reducing hallucination. It is important that the text is taken in its original form without any abridgement or reformulation.

steps.title: Step 3: Lean on the quote to answer
steps.body: Have them answer questions based on the quotes they selected. Now the answer is not the model's memory, but the sentences we just pulled out. When writing an answer, you may also be given instructions to limit external knowledge, such as not to use general knowledge outside the document.

steps.title: Step 4: Provide a source for each claim, and retract if you cannot find it.
steps.body: Include citations and sources for each claim so you can audit the response. After writing a response, you can have students find citations to support each claim and, if they cannot find one, withdraw their claim. Responses requiring evidence become easier for humans to verify. This is because you only need to compare the sentences next to the citation.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the basic techniques, let's look at more advanced validation techniques and how to deal with long output.

screens.title: Advanced verification techniques and handling long outputs
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare results to see questionable verification techniques and how to create lengthy outputs.

tabs.label: Compare multiple times
tabs.body:
Run the same prompt multiple times to see if the results match. This is what you might call a consistency check. The purpose is different from the Best-of-N technique, which selects the best one among several candidates. The Claude article explains that any discrepancy between the outputs is seen as a sign that there may be hallucination. Answers based on facts tend to repeat the same information even if given multiple times, while made-up answers tend to change each time.

The SelfCheckGPT paper also starts from the same idea. We believed that if the model knew something, multiple answers would share the same fact, and that made-up facts would tend to diverge and conflict with each response, so we used this to detect hallucination without external data. Self-consistency, a related technique, is a method of selecting the most consistent answer by drawing multiple inference paths, and has been reported to improve performance on reasoning tasks.

For example, if you ask for the termination conditions of a contract five times and the same conditions come up each time, it is trustworthy, but items that are sometimes present and sometimes not are subjects that a person must check against the original text. However, just because it matches does not mean it is correct. A match is only a signal of trustworthiness and not a substitute for fact-checking, as the model may repeat the same errors.

tabs.label: repeat purification
tabs.body:
The previous output is used as input for the next prompt to be verified or supplemented. For example, it asks, 'Check whether each sentence in the summary above has a basis in the original text, and mark sentences that have no basis.' The documentation explains that this method helps catch and fix contradictions.

Rather than trying to come up with a complete answer all at once, the approach is to split it into two stages: drafting and checking.

tabs.label: Thought Summary Review
tabs.body:
Turn on the thinking function and take the reasoning summarized as `display: "summarized"`. When an answer seems strange, read the summarized reasoning in the thinking block to find any faulty logic or assumptions, Claude's article advises.

For example, if the thought summary reveals that the model misread the terms of a contract, you can add instructions to correct that point. Please remember that what you see here is a summary, not the original text.

Additionally, there is no guarantee that the thoughts you see are a direct record of the model's actual judgment process. Studies have reported cases where the explanation does not reveal what caused the model to change its answer. Therefore, the summary of thoughts is only used as a clue to indicate where to doubt, and the correct and incorrect points are checked against the original text.

tabs.label: long output
tabs.body:
One model call generates up to approximately 64K tokens. Gemini 4 Argon's long decode generates 64K token units in succession for long responses that exceed this limit and combines them into one response.

To write, you must turn on background execution with `background: true` and set `max_output_tokens` greater than 65,536. The server then picks up the next fragment from where the previous one left off, and you poll or stream the results.

Since input, thoughts, and output all share a unified context window, you also need to consider that the longer you want to output, the less space you have for your input and thoughts.

screens.outro: Now that we've introduced all of the techniques, let's move on to an explanation that identifies the causes of errors.

ext.title: Manakul et al., SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
Wang et al., Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
Turpin et al., Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting

screens.title: Case Commentary 1: Identifying Where Errors Come From
screens.lead: When you select a case card, the instructor's basis for classifying the cause and prescriptions are revealed. First, determine for yourself which is the cause and then press it.

items.prompt: Case A: Each response is a mixture of tables, lists, and paragraphs.
items.answer: This is a problem caused by the lack of format instructions and examples. The model wasn't given the desired look, so it had to be picked anew each time. The prescription is to define the output format as JSON or a template, and show one or two examples of the desired output. This is an issue that has nothing to do with the accuracy of the facts.

items.prompt: Case B: Item name changes every time
items.answer: This is a problem of fixing the structure with example/structured output. The format is generally similar, but the column names are changed, such as 'Article', 'Condition', and 'Content'. The prescription is to specify the column names as examples and output schema. Prefill is used as an auxiliary method only on models that support it. The model will follow the specified item name.

items.prompt: Case C: Conditions that are not in the document are included
items.answer: It is a problem of lack of evidence and lack of acceptance of ‘don’t know’. The model filled in the blanks even though it had no basis in the documentation. The prescription is to allow the answer to be absent if it is not in the document, to select the original citation first, and to include a citation for each claim. Even if you fix the format, this problem remains.

items.prompt: If you summarize your judgment criteria in one line, what would they be?
items.answer: If the format is shaky, we turn to instructions and examples, and if the facts are wrong, we turn to requests for evidence. If you first look at the symptoms, determine the location of the cause, and then write a prescription appropriate for that location, you will spend less time fixing the wrong thing. When both problems appear together, both treatments are applied. For example, if your table format is shaky and has missing clauses mixed in, you should fix the look with format definitions and supported structured output while also requiring supporting citations.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the causes, let us explain step by step the process of reducing factual errors.

screens.title: Case Commentary 2: Reducing hallucination using an evidence-required approach
screens.lead: The instructor improves the contract termination conditions questions step by step. Select the arrows to follow how the answers change as instructions are added one by one.

steps.title: original prompt
steps.body: The original is like this: 'Please tell me the terms of termination of this contract.' The response included conditions such as 30 days prior notice of termination and 10% penalty, but the penalty clause was not in the contract. The model is filled with what a typical contract looks like.

steps.title: Step 1: Permission not to know
steps.body: Add one more line of instructions. 'If it is not in the contract, please answer 'not in the document.' Now the model has a way to say there is nothing instead of filling in the blank. Just this one line significantly reduces the number of unfounded conditions.

steps.title: Step 2: Quote the original text first.
steps.body: Add the following instructions: 'First, quote the sentences related to termination directly from the contract.' The model must obtain the actual sentences before summarizing the terms, making it difficult to insert content that is not in the contract.

steps.title: Step 3: Attach a citation and withdraw if not found.
steps.body: Add a third instruction. 'Attach the appropriate citation next to each termination condition, and withdraw any condition for which you cannot find a citation.' The 10 percent penalty clause is now withdrawn due to lack of supporting text. Even when a human is checking, the quotation and conditions can be compared side by side.

steps.title: Confirm by repeating step 4
steps.body: Finally, we run the same request multiple times. Conditions where the results are the same every time are reliable, and items that vary are directly compared to the original text by humans. This is because discrepancies can be a sign of hallucination.

steps.title: final prompt
steps.body:
```
Please find the termination conditions in the following contract.
1. If it is not in the contract, answer “not in the document.”
2. First quote the sentence related to termination in its original text.
3. Attach the appropriate citation next to each termination condition,
   Please withdraw terms for which you cannot find a citation.
4. Do not use general knowledge outside of the contract.

<contract>
(Original text of contract)
</contract>
```

The reason the instructions became longer was not because they were wordy, but because the evidence was strengthened step by step.

screens.outro: Now that we've finished the case, let's summarize the main points of this lesson.

screens.title: Determine the location of the cause by symptoms
screens.lead: Let's organize the techniques covered in this class by connecting them to the first question.

paragraphs: The first question was how to determine whether the error came from instructions, examples, or lack of evidence. Now there are standards. If the shape of your response falters, anchor the structure with formatting instructions, examples, and supported structured output. If the facts are incorrect, the answer is included in the document with permission to not know, citing the original text, and providing evidence.

Consistency in repetitive tasks is achieved by changing the structure of instructions, not by making them longer. Base it on a fixed set of information, break complex tasks into subtasks, and anchor roles with system prompts.

Still, any remaining doubts are filtered out by comparing the results. Points to check include changes made by repeating the same request multiple times, contradictions revealed by re-verifying the previous output, and incorrect assumptions seen in the thought summary. The final check is done by a human comparing it with the original text.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: If the format is incorrect, check the instructions and examples first, and if the facts are incorrect, check the supporting evidence first.

checks.q: When I asked about the contract's termination conditions, I got mixed up with conditions that were not in the document. What would be the first instruction worth adding?
options: Instructions to ‘write the termination conditions longer and more detailed’
Output format instructions to ‘organize in a table’
Instructions to ‘fill in the missing conditions by mobilizing all your common sense’
Permission to say ‘if it is not in the document, you can answer ‘not in the document’
checks.explain: Just giving yourself permission to say you don't know can significantly reduce false information. In fact, errors arise not from format but from lack of evidence.

wrong.0: Increasing the length does not add any evidence and may actually make the content longer.
wrong.1: Formal instructions are a prescription for format shakiness, not factual errors.
wrong.2: Mobilizing external knowledge further blends content outside the document.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match the following symptoms with the prescription:
left: Each response contains a jumble of tables, lists, and paragraphs.
Conditions that are not in the document are included.
right: Requesting evidence and allowing ‘I don’t know’
Fix the structure with example/structured output
checks.explain: Format fluctuations are approached with instructions and examples, fixing item names are approached with examples and pre-fills, and factual errors are approached with a request for evidence.
checks.intro: Let’s check what we looked at earlier with one problem. There are no records or grading, so feel free to solve it.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

checks.q: Try to put the flow in the right order to reduce the problem of termination conditions not in the contract.
items: If it is not in the document, allow the answer ‘not in the document’
Sentences related to termination should be extracted in their original text first.
Have them put a citation next to each condition and withdraw it if they can't find it.
By executing the same request multiple times, a person checks for items that produce different results.
checks.explain: The evidence is strengthened step by step in the order of acceptance, extraction of original text citations, attachment and withdrawal of citations, and human verification after repeated execution.
checks.intro: Please choose with the intention of organizing what you have learned. Results are not saved.

glossary.def: This is a technique that fills in the beginning of the model response in advance so that it follows the desired format. Support varies depending on model and provider.
This is an instruction to include an original quote or source for each claim. If you can't find any evidence, you can have the claim withdrawn.

This method runs the same prompt several times and checks whether the responses agree. Disagreement can indicate hallucination, but agreement does not guarantee accuracy. It differs from Best-of-N, which selects the best response from several candidates.
This is a function where Gemini 4 Argon generates a series of long outputs exceeding 64K tokens and combines them into one response.

This is a function that forces the structure of the response by passing the JSON schema to the API. Even if the structure is correct, it does not mean that the meaning of the value is also correct, so the values ​​are verified separately.

misconceptions.myth: The reasons why the answers are wrong are all the same.
misconceptions.fact: Format errors often come from instructions and examples, and factual errors often come from lack of evidence. To be effective, a prescription must be appropriate for the location of the cause.

misconceptions.myth: If you make them say they don't know, they will be less helpful.
misconceptions.fact: Just giving yourself permission to say you don't know can significantly reduce false information. A response that says there is nothing is more useful at work than a response that makes up something that is not there.

misconceptions.myth: Any number of long outputs can be produced with a single call.
misconceptions.fact: There is an output limit for one call. Gemini 4 Argon uses a separate method of creating 64K token units by concatenating them with long decode.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The output format is set as template/example/structured output, and prefill checks whether the model is supported.
Linking searches, linking prompts, and maintaining roles are structural ways to increase consistency.
Requiring evidence and allowing ‘if you don’t know, you don’t know’ are basic measures to reduce hallucination.
We first distinguish whether the error comes from instructions, examples, or evidence, and then prescribe it.

closing.reflection: If there is a task in my work where the AI result format is unstable and post-processing is cumbersome, which format do I want to fix first?
